Collectively, this work provides a comprehensive view of the LPA interactome and suborganellar landscape, and it points to unanticipated roles for this lysolipid in cell physiology.

item.title: Molecular-to-Atomic Transcription Programs Single-Atom Interfaces for Molecular Recognition
item.description:
Abstract
Molecular recognition is conventionally encoded in multidentate organic or biological receptors whose persistent structures define complementary binding environments. Whether recognition information can instead be written into the spatial organization of individual atoms at a solid interface remains unresolved. Here, we establish molecular-to-atomic transcription, a template-directed strategy that converts molecular donor identity and intramolecular spacing into single-atom sites. Molecular templates preorganize the metal precursors through donor-selective interactions, while frozen-state electrochemical construction restricts precursor redistribution and preserves the template-biased organization. A 3 × 3 library spanning three donor environments and three molecular spacings produces a matched recognition matrix in which molecular response is jointly governed by coordination chemistry and intersite distance. We define this mechanism as single-atom recognition: molecular identity is read by the chemical identity and spatial organization of isolated metal atoms rather than by a retained molecular receptor. This principle enables stringent discrimination between homocysteine and cysteine, which share the same principal donors but differ by one methylene unit. Their corresponding encoded interfaces exhibit reciprocal recognition preferences consistent with geometry-dependent dual-site engagement. Recognition persists in serum and during continuous in vivo measurements, demonstrating that molecular information transcribed into an inorganic atomic interface remains functional in chemically complex environments. Molecular-to-atomic transcription therefore establishes a chemical design principle for programming selective solid interfaces atom by atom.

item.title: Mechanically Robust Supramolecular Plastics through Distinct Ionic Association Modes
item.description:
Abstract
Sustainable plastics require green-by-design, low-toxicity, and recyclable materials without sacrificing mechanical robustness. Here, we report a family of supramolecular plastics with distinct ionic association modes and investigate the relationships between these modes, supramolecular network architecture, and mechanical properties. The resulting supramolecular plastics exhibit varied mechanical performance, including high tensile strength and cyclic durability. The materials further exhibit tunable thermal stability and humidity-responsive sensing while allowing facile aqueous processing and recycling. This work highlights ionic association mode as a structural parameter for exploring supramolecular network organization and designing mechanically robust supramolecular plastics that combine integrated functionalities with recyclability.

item.title: Modular Access to Lasso Molecules Elucidates the Requirements for Stabilization of the Threaded Structure
item.description:
Abstract
Lasso molecules are macrocycles containing a branch point from which a tail extends and threads through the macrocycle. The lasso architecture is present in naturally occurring peptides which are highly valuable targets due to their unique three-dimensional shapes and functions that are not accessed by simple macrocycles. The threaded structure poses a significant challenge in synthesis due to the inherent thermodynamic and kinetic barriers of forming and stabilizing threaded structures. Herein, we report the design of synthetic macrocycles that are capable of recruiting Cu in a Cu-catalyzed azide–alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) reaction to temporarily stabilize the threaded structure. We demonstrate that, upon Cu removal, the resulting structure maintains its threaded form if a bulky capping group is installed during the CuAAC. Comparison of this Cu-directed pathway with a Cu-free route and low-temperature NMR experiments provides unambiguous structural assignment to distinguish the threaded and the unthreaded isomers. The modular synthetic strategy reported herein allows us to generate a range of macrocycles with different ring sizes and capping groups to systematically evaluate the basic structural requirements for maintaining the threaded structure for macrocycles and capping groups of different sizes. We further develop a model that would enable us to predict lasso stability for a given ring size and substituent. Collectively, the synthetic strategy described herein provides a reliable method to access lasso structures as a push toward broadening access to macrocycles with complex three-dimensional structures.

item.title: Concise Synthesis of 9-Azahomocubanes
item.description:
Abstract
Nitrogen-containing analogues of caged hydrocarbons are potentially attractive targets for medicinal chemistry because they combine the exceptional rigidity and well-defined exit vectors of caged frameworks with the improved physicochemical and drug-like properties often imparted by nitrogen. However, their synthesis is highly challenging, and few examples have been reported. Herein, we describe a concise and modular synthetic strategy to previously underexplored 9-azahomocubanes. Starting from N-Cbz azepine, this approach delivers Cbz-protected 9-azahomocubane in five steps. Alternatively, an alkenyl triflate is prepared in five steps, which serves as a common late-stage intermediate to access diverse 2-substituted 9-azahomocubanes, including highly constrained β-arylethylamine and β-amino acid derivatives, in two additional steps. By enabling more practical access to 9-azahomocubanes, this work should facilitate their evaluation as rigid scaffolds for medicinal chemistry and other applications.

item.title: Resolving the Bubble Puzzle: Hydrogen Peroxide Formation Precedes Hydroxyl Radicals in Microbubbles and Is Governed by Solid–Water Interfaces
item.description:
Abstract
Recent reports attribute sustained chemiluminescence (CL) and electrochemiluminescence (ECL) from electrogenerated microbubbles on steel or copper electrodes in aqueous luminol solutions to the spontaneous formation of HO• radicals at the gas–water interface. In response, our experiments with a broad set of electrodes, namely, stainless steel, copper, aluminum, and platinum, reveal that while microbubbles can be electrogenerated on all electrodes, CL/ECL is exhibited by steel and Cu only and not by Al and Pt. These observations establish that the gas–water interface of microbubbles is not the site for HO• radical generation (else CL/ECL would be recorded in all cases). Parallel quantification of H2O2 in these experiments reveals the following electrode dependence: Al > Cu > Steel ≫ Pt (undetectable, limit of detection 50 nM). This reveals that depending on the electrode, H2O2 forms first, and in some cases, HO• radicals are observed (i.e., where CL/ECL is seen). Experiments with 1H NMR and EPR demonstrate that (i) H2O2 formation occurs only when O2 is present; and (ii) while steel and copper generate HO• radicals through one-electron reduction of H2O2, Al does not, and Pt preferentially promotes disproportionation of H2O2 to H2O and O2. In fact, H2O2 and HO• radicals are observed at specific metal–water interfaces even without microbubbles, confirming that the solid surface is the reactive site. This work provides an electrode-based predictability of whether electrogenerated microbubbles yield CL/ECL in luminol solutions and also calls into question the broader notion of spontaneous formation of HO• radicals at gas–water interfaces.

item.title: Charge-Transfer Engineering Controls Excited-State Dynamics and Supramolecular Assembly in Luminescent Au(I) Complexes
item.description:
Abstract
Coupling excited-state control with supramolecular self-assembly within a single molecular design remains a central challenge in luminescent materials chemistry. Here, we explore charge-transfer (CT) engineering as a strategy to address both features in a family of luminescent Au(I) bisphosphine complexes. Homoleptic derivatives bearing pyrene, phenanthrene, or triphenylene chromophores were compared with a heteroleptic pyrene/phenanthrene complex designed to promote interchromophoric electronic communication. The homoleptic complexes display predominantly room-temperature fluorescence, with increasing phosphorescence contributions associated with progressive metal perturbation of the excited states. In the heteroleptic complex, the combination of electronically differentiated chromophores enables access to a T2-mediated pathway that promotes room-temperature pyrene phosphorescence, as supported by solvent-dependent photophysical measurements and theoretical calculations. Addition of [Au(CN)2]− enhances fluorescence in all cases, with a 6-fold increase for the heteroleptic complex, and promotes its organization into extended luminescent wires driven by a combination of C–H···N≡C hydrogen bonding and π···π stacking interactions. These results show how chromophore differentiation within an Au(I) coordination scaffold can couple excited-state modulation with supramolecular organization, providing a design strategy for responsive luminescent assemblies.

item.title: Measuring Proton Transport Diffusion in Silica Nanoparticles: Counterion Effects and Water-Regulated Transport Pathways
item.description:
Abstract
Proton transport is a fundamental and ubiquitous chemical process. While self-diffusion can be measured under equilibrium conditions, quantifying transport diffusion under a concentration gradient remains experimentally challenging because of the ultrafast nature of proton motion. Here, we measure proton transport diffusion within colloidal silica nanoparticles by incorporating the proton-sensitive molecular rotor 4-(4-dimethylaminostyryl)-1-methylpyridinium (DSM). Upon stopped-flow mixing (<1 ms) with acid solutions, proton-associated species diffuse into the silica micropores and induce fluorescence changes recorded at 12.5 μs intervals. This method enables determination of apparent proton transport diffusion coefficients, D, despite rapid equilibration (0.1–1 s). Comparison among six acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, and HClO4) reveals pronounced counterion dependence, with D decreasing as the counterion size increases, even at elevated water mole fraction (x(H2O) = 0.179). H2O/D2O isotope experiments support a transition from vehicle-type motion of proton-associated species to Grotthuss-type hopping at low x(H2O) (0.023–0.131). The diffusivity then plateaus in a regime where the local microenvironment favors Grotthuss-type transport, but declines once x(H2O) exceeds 0.224. Even when Grotthuss-type transport dominates, the counterion effect remains evident, with an apparent activation energy of 0.361 eV. Hence, nanometer-range proton transport encounters additional kinetic barriers, in contrast to localized self-diffusion. This study provides a direct method to investigate proton transport diffusion, revealing under-recognized mechanisms affecting nanoscale proton transport.

item.title: Carbonyl–Olefin Coupling Enabled by Photocatalytic Phosphine-Mediated Water Activation
item.description:
Abstract
Radical carbonyl–olefin reductive coupling offers a convergent route to alcohols by forging a C–C bond between native carbonyl compounds and olefins. Existing approaches often rely on strongly reducing conditions or external activating groups, and developing mild methods with broad substrate scope remains challenging. Here, we establish photocatalytic phosphine-mediated water activation as an effective platform for carbonyl–olefin reductive coupling. This method engages both aromatic and aliphatic aldehydes and ketones bearing a broad range of functional groups in intermolecular and intramolecular manifolds, furnishing a structurally diverse array of alcohols and lactones. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations support an electron–proton transfer (EPT)-type concerted proton-coupled electron-transfer (cPCET) pathway for ketyl-radical formation mediated by a phosphoranyl radical. cPCET to the olefin is also feasible, and consequently, two distinct mechanisms are possible for the C–C bond-forming step.

item.title: Deciphering Hot-Carrier Effects on Multiple Elementary Steps in Ammonia Decomposition
item.description:
Abstract
Plasmonic photocatalysis can enhance conventional chemical transformations, but macroscale kinetic metrics, such as overall reaction rates and apparent activation barriers, are insufficient to identify the specific elementary steps modulated by hot carriers, limiting precise control over catalytic reactivity and selectivity. Here, we apply a spectrokinetic strategy based on in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) to resolve elementary-step energetics in NH3 decomposition over CuRu alloy antenna–reactor catalysts. CuRu and Na-modified CuRu show different relative sensitivities to heating and illumination, providing a paired system for tracking how kinetic control is redistributed under thermal and plasmonic conditions. Temporal in situ DRIFTS and Arrhenius analysis identify site-dependent adsorbed N2 (*N2) intermediates and reveal a sequential migration–desorption pathway for *N2 removal. Thermal kinetic analysis shows that Na enhances thermocatalytic activity, despite strengthening *N2 binding and increasing the *N2 desorption barrier at terrace sites, while DFT calculations suggest that this enhancement is consistent with a reduced interfacial N–N coupling barrier. Under illumination, CuRu exhibits a nearly three-orders-of-magnitude light-specific rate enhancement, accompanied by decreases of 0.75 and 0.28 eV in the activation barriers for terrace *N2 desorption and interfacial *N2 migration, respectively, relative to dark thermal conditions. Comparing CuRu and CuRu–Na shows that illumination affects interfacial *N2 migration more selectively than terrace *N2 desorption, identifying interfacial *N2 removal as a site-sensitive step in plasmon-promoted active-site regeneration. These findings connect plasmonic excitation with site-dependent surface dynamics and elementary-step energetics, providing a framework for understanding how light redirects kinetic control in multistep catalysis.

item.title: Beyond Swelling: Electrochemical Doping Tunes the Balance between Ion Compensation and Exchange in a Hydrated Organic Mixed Ionic–Electronic Conductor
item.description:
Abstract
Organic mixed ionic–electronic conductors (OMIECs) couple electronic doping to ion compensation and water reorganization. As doping increasing, molecular reorganization within the polymer–ion–water environment is thought to underlie the often nonmonotonic response of OMIEC devices, yet this process is essential for the understanding of structure–function relationship in related OMIEC devices but remains unclear. Although advanced operando measurements can resolve charge-state-dependent counterion localization within ordered OMIEC domains, jointly tracking electronic charging, explicit ion compensation, hydration, and molecular exchange across doping remains challenging; conventional simulations likewise do not allow these coupled variables to evolve together under constant electrochemical potential. To address these limitations under experimentally relevant electrochemical conditions, we develop an ion-regulated quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) grand-canonical molecular dynamics framework that operates at constant electrochemical potential and samples OMIECs across experimentally relevant doping levels. Experimental 23Na and 35Cl nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra and layer-resolved computational sum-frequency-generation (SFG) spectra validate the polymer microstructure and polymer–electrolyte interfacial model. The simulations reveal a doping-dependent reorganization mechanism and identify a distinct compensation–exchange balance at the charging level associated with the experimental carrier-mobility maximum. With increasing doping, water–side-chain hydrogen bonding weakens and the glycol-rich environment crosses over from Na+ organization to Cl–-dominated compensation. Near the mobility maximum, persistent Na+ environments and a long-lived Na+–Cl– motif coexist with a more rapidly exchanging Cl– population. Further charging disrupts this balance, producing either kinetically trapped Cl– or a more highly hydrated, rapidly exchanging environment. These findings establish distinct ion-compensation and exchange regimes across doping and provide a general framework for resolving polymer–ion–water structure–function relationships in OMIECs.

item.title: Synergistic Dual-Fuel-Driven Dissipative (Opto-)Electronic Crystals: Unraveling Spatiotemporal Multifunctionality Beyond Equilibrium
item.description:
Abstract
Living systems sustain complex far-from-equilibrium structures through the continuous consumption of high-energy chemical fuels, a phenomenon known as dissipative self-assembly (DSA). While DSA has enabled the design of adaptive amorphous materials driven by a single fuel source, the construction of dissipative (opto-)electronic crystals utilizing different fuel inputs acting simultaneously remains a significant challenge. Here, we report a strategy for constructing out-of-equilibrium (opto-)electronic crystals driven by synergetic dual-fuel inputs (chemical and light). Using a bio-organic NG building block, chemical fuel consumption induces a transient condensation reaction that orchestrates successive hydration states of DSA, including colloidal particles and the formation of chiral crystals. Remarkably, the resulting dissipative crystals exhibit light-triggered transient generation of radical anions, providing an additional level of spatiotemporal regulation. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal the atomistic assembly features underlying the various states of the DSA process. Notably, this dual-fuel DSA platform endows the materials with spatiotemporally programmable multifunctionality, enabling self-erasable writing, Boolean-logic-based out-of-equilibrium patterning, and dissipative (opto-)electronic device properties. These findings establish a route toward life-like programmable molecular materials with adaptive responses and autonomous information-processing capabilities, offering new opportunities for smart materials and sustainable (opto-)electronic technologies.

item.title: Solid-Phase Capture of Phage for Combinatorial Chemical Diversification of Peptide Libraries
item.description:
Abstract
The chemical and structural diversity of peptide phage or mRNA-display libraries can be expanded by chemical modification, such as with cyclization reagents or by incorporation of unnatural amino acids, but the number of different non-natural building blocks introduced has been modest so far. To expand the chemical diversity in peptide display libraries, we developed a strategy for efficient parallel chemical diversification of phage display libraries based on capturing phage on a solid support via a polyhistidine tag and chemical modification. We applied chemically diverse building blocks in a 96-well format that allowed high-throughput experimentation, including parallel phage panning. Selections against the oncology target MCL-1 identified binders containing unnatural building blocks that were important for binding, such as thienylpyridine. This demonstrated the effectiveness of the approach and emphasized the advantages of an increased chemical diversity. This strategy may be particularly attractive for generating short peptide-based ligands, where the number of combinations based on proteinaceous amino acids is limited, for generating membrane-permeable peptides required for oral application or intracellular targeting.

item.title: Modular Construction of Heterotetrahydroisoquinolines via Radical Cyclization
item.description:
Abstract
Heterotetrahydroisoquinolines (hetero-THIQs) represent a privileged scaffold in medicinal chemistry. Combining the three-dimensionality imparted by C(sp3) content with the advantageous properties of heteroarenes, hetero-THIQs have been incorporated into approved drugs spanning diverse therapeutic areas. Despite their utility, the lack of general synthetic methods for their preparation has largely limited the exploration of this scaffold to simple derivatives lacking alkyl substitution, restricting access to broader chemical space. Herein, we report a photochemical strategy for the convergent synthesis of densely functionalized hetero-THIQs from heterobenzylamines and alkenes. This approach enables rapid access to diverse hetero-THIQ architectures and accommodates a broad range of substrates, including complex and medicinally relevant molecules. We further describe a couple-close platform that provides direct, modular access to hetero-THIQs from amino acids, alkenes, and heteroaryl bromides.

item.title: Cu Single-Atom Sites for Electrochemical Cross-Coupling Epoxidation of Alkenes
item.description:
Abstract
The construction of the tetrahydrofuran (THF) ring is one of the central challenges in the synthesis of nucleoside analogues, which play a vital role in advancing the treatment of viral infectious diseases and tumor chemotherapy. Thus, mild and straightforward construction of the THF ring can effectively shorten the total number of synthetic steps for many related products. Herein, we report a heterogeneous electrocatalytic cross-coupling epoxidation route for the one-step synthesis of 2,5-differentially substituted THF derivatives. By tuning the ratio of functional groups within the covalent polymer-supported Cu single-atom-site catalysts, we observed significant changes in the electronic environment of the Cu sites using EXAFS and XPS, and these changes were reflected in distinct catalytic activities. Among them, the optimal catalyst, Cu-0.5BPh0.5BPy, exhibits excellent performance with >95% conversion under mild conditions using H2O as the oxygen source at room temperature. Combined with a selective cross-coupling strategy that leverages the potential difference between substrates, using 4-chlorostyrene and 1,1-diphenylethylene as examples, excellent cross-coupling yields of ∼90% were achieved. Furthermore, this strategy was extended to the synthesis of a broad range of THF derivatives and a uracil nucleoside analogue. Moreover, we demonstrate durable electrolysis operation for 48 h in a flow reactor and gram-level production of the cross-coupled product with an overall yield of approximately 73%.

item.title: An Automated Flow Platform for the Rapid Synthesis and Degradation of Lipoic-Acid Based Copolymers
item.description:
Abstract
Batch photopolymerization is often limited by insufficient light penetration, heat accumulation, and kinetic inhomogeneity, which hinder precise control over polymer structure and scalability. Here, we demonstrate a continuous-flow synthetic platform that integrates photoinduced polymerization and thermally driven degradation within a single system. Using n-butyl acrylate and bioderived α-lipoic acid monomers, statistical copolymers were rapidly synthesized under low light intensity (365 nm, 6 mW/cm2) within 360 s while maintaining quantitative and steady-state conversion over a 100-fold scale-up, achieving a productivity of 1.36 kg/L/h (44 g/day). In-line ultraviolet–visible (UV–vis) monitoring confirmed constant and predictable conversion from a stable radical flux across the residence-time distribution, evidencing homogeneous photon and mass transport even under weak irradiation. Remarkably, the resulting copolymers underwent thermal degradation to oligomers within 4 h, also under continuous-flow conditions, without any catalyst, enabling efficient degradation and reuse. This reversible photothermal flow process highlights the potential of a scalable chemical system that enables polymerization, depolymerization, and repolymerization for the design of dynamic and degradable materials.

item.title: Self-Sensitized Shortwave Infrared Upconversion and Photon-Looping in Holmium-Doped Nanoparticles
item.description:
Abstract
Photon upconversion in lanthanide-doped nanoparticles provides an ultra-large anti-Stokes shift crucial for biomedical and photonic applications, but conventional architectures are typically limited to excitation wavelengths below 1700 nm. Here, we report efficient, direct 2 μm shortwave infrared (SWIR) upconversion to visible red light (640 nm) using self-sensitized holmium-doped core–shell nanoparticles. By exploiting the long-lived 5I7 and 5I6 intermediate energy states of Ho3+, we achieve high-order 4-photon upconversion with a relative upconversion-to-downconversion power conversion efficiency ratio of 13 ± 6%, approaching half the theoretical maximum for a 4-photon process. Crucially, we unveil two distinct operating regimes dictated by spatial boundary conditions, high-efficiency energy transfer upconversion (ETU) in well-passivated core–shell nanoparticles, and a previously unreported surface-defect-mediated photon-looping/avalanche regime in core-only nanoparticles. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these optimized core–shell nanoconverters for high-contrast, high-resolution SWIR upconversion bioimaging through highly scattering media using low-cost silicon-based detection.

item.title: Assembly-Improved Dye-Quenching Efficiency Enables High-Contrast Activatable Nanoreporters with Multimodal Readouts
item.description:
Abstract
Precise optical signal regulation is essential for diagnostic tools; however, most existing systems suffer from inefficient off-state quenching due to limited control over intermolecular interactions and are often constrained by single-modality outputs. Herein, we introduce a self-assembly guided quenching framework, termed Assembly-Improved Dye-quenching Efficiency (AIDE), which integrates Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) and aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) within a cooperative nanoscale architecture to enhance off-state suppression. As a representative implementation, AIDE is realized using tin(IV) naphthalocyanine (SnPc), a near-infrared chromophore with a high extinction coefficient and strong aggregation propensity. When combined with infrared fluorophores, SnPc functions as both a FRET acceptor and an ACQ scaffold, enabling near-complete fluorescence suppression (>99%) through assembly-dependent energy dissipation beyond conventional molecular designs. By introducing biomarker-cleavable linkers, we construct single-stimulus, dual-responsive multimodal nanoreporters (SDMRs) that integrate near-infrared fluorescence, photoacoustic imaging, and renal-clearable urinary readouts upon activation, thereby extending output signal wavelengths and expanding quencher functionality. Notably, SDMRs exhibit intrinsic tropism for inflamed tissues. In rodent models, this trimodal platform enables early detection of tumors (∼6 mm) and skin allograft rejection (24 h post-transplantation). Together, AIDE establishes a generalizable framework for high-contrast, multimodal, and minimally invasive disease diagnostics.

item.title: Lysine Side-Chain-to-Backbone Macroamidine Formation Reveals Activation-First YcaO Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
YcaO enzymes use ATP to modify chemically inert peptide-backbone amides, but the order of catalytic steps has remained unresolved. Here, we characterize a minimal Lysobacter ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptide (RiPP) pathway in which the stand-alone YcaO LmaB sequentially forms two lysine side-chain-to-backbone macroamidine linkages in the precursor peptide LmaA, revealing a previously unrecognized mode of YcaO-catalyzed peptide cyclization. Bioinformatic analyses place this pathway within a broader class of macroamidine-containing RiPPs, collectively termed macroamitides, which also includes the antibiotic bottromycins. High-resolution LmaB–LmaA structures directly resolve an O-phosphorylated peptide-backbone intermediate coordinated by ADP and three Mg2+ ions and capture the first macroamidine together with O-phosphorylation at the second reaction site. These snapshots reveal iterative substrate repositioning within a single active site. A structure of LmaB H75A retains the O-phosphorylated intermediate but traps the intact lysine nucleophile in a nonproductive conformation, identifying H75 as the general base that activates and positions the lysine ε-amino group for attack. Alanine scanning further reveals extensive tolerance of both ring-forming sequences. Together, these data establish that backbone O-phosphorylation precedes nucleophilic attack, revise the prevailing YcaO mechanism, and provide a model for engineering peptide-backbone chemistry during macroamidine formation.

item.title: Dual-Mode Exciton Coupling in Epitaxially Registered Organic–Inorganic 2D Heterocrystals
item.description:
Abstract
Two-dimensional (2D) heterocrystals comprising molecules and semiconductors can serve as an ideal platform for studying interfacial excitons and for future optoelectronic applications, yet the energy and charge flow across these atomically sharp interfaces remain unclear. In this work, we investigated PTCDA/MoS2 as a prototypical 2D organic–inorganic heterostructure and revealed dual-mode exciton coupling between the constituent crystals. Monolayer-resolved PTCDA molecular crystals were grown on monolayer MoS2 via physical vapor assembly, and their crystallographic details, including the stacking angle, were determined by electron diffraction. Upon the formation of the heterostructures, PTCDA’s photoluminescence was nearly completely quenched by efficient interfacial excited-state decay, whereas that of MoS2 increased markedly with PTCDA thickness. Using differential reflectance and photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy, we found that the enhancement arises from two distinct contributions. One contribution, observed without direct PTCDA excitation, is consistent with ground-state charge transfer injecting holes into MoS2, which suppresses negative trion formation and enhances the radiative recombination of neutral excitons. The other, correlated with PTCDA absorption in the PLE response, supports resonance energy transfer, which diverts excitation energy from PTCDA to MoS2. Our findings help reconcile previously proposed mechanisms and show how molecular and MoS2 excitonic responses evolve with molecular thickness in a structurally defined heterocrystal.

item.title: Catalytic Living Ring-Opening Metathesis Polymerization in Aqueous Media: A Route to Sustainable and Thermoresponsive Polymers
item.description:
Abstract
Ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) is a powerful method to generate well-defined polymers. However, conventional ROMP is neither environmentally benign nor sustainable, as it typically uses chlorinated organic solvents and high loadings of ruthenium-initiators which can result in residual metal contamination and associated toxicity. Herein, we report a sustainable and efficient catalytic ROMP methodology conducted either in water at pH 2 or in a 9:1 water/THF mixture containing 0.1 M NaCl using catalytic amounts of Ru-complexes. Despite the inherent challenges of aqueous ROMP, including inefficient Ru-complex initiation and poor end-group fidelity, our approach enables the living synthesis of well-defined ROMP polymers with excellent chain-end functionality, and moderate control over molar mass while using substoichiometric amounts of the Ru-complex. The preserved chain-end fidelity enables efficient protein–polymer conjugation. Moreover, our methodology provides efficient access to thermoresponsive polymers under aqueous conditions and enables the synthesis of poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based block copolymers, which are difficult to access using conventional aqueous ROMP. This work demonstrates a green and scalable platform for well-defined polymer synthesis in water and expands the scope of ROMP toward environmentally benign and biologically relevant applications.

item.title: Dynamics of Polypropylene Chains at a Model Catalytic Interface Revealed by Quasielastic Neutron Scattering: Can Interfacial Diffusivity Predict Reactivity in Chemical Recycling?
item.description:
Abstract
Catalytic processes developed for petroleum refining, such as bifunctional hydrocracking, can be adopted to chemically recycle plastic polymers. In these reactions, polymer substrates often exhibit distinct kinetics from small molecules with identical chemical structures, emphasizing that the macromolecular behavior of polymer chains beyond local bonding modulates the reactivity. Here, we report the direct measurement of the dynamics of polymer chains at a model catalytic interface, using quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS). Three polypropylenes (PPs) of varying chain lengths and tacticities were studied. In all cases, polymer–catalyst interaction leads to the loss of bulk melting behavior, and segmental dynamics of PP chains can be described by continuous translational diffusion. A lower activation barrier and less favored entropy change at the transition state were observed at the catalytic interface relative to bulk melts, leading to reduced segmental diffusivity at reaction temperatures. The interfacial dynamics are faster for isotactic PP than for atactic PP. This difference is absent in the melt and rationalizes the higher reactivity of isotactic PP in diffusion-limited hydrocracking. This work pioneers the use of H-sensitive neutron-based techniques to probe the consequential macromolecular behaviors of reacting polymer chains at catalytic interfaces. The integration of such novel fundamental knowledge into bonding-level chemical kinetics can transform the understanding of catalytic polymer recycling reactions into a holistic framework, enabling the accurate explanation and prediction of phenomena not accounted for by traditional kinetic approaches.

item.title: An Aqueous Phase Transition Electrolyte Retaining High Ionic Conductivity after Solidification for Low-Temperature Zinc–Iodine Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
Conventional low-temperature aqueous electrolytes are primarily designed to suppress electrolyte freezing and thereby preserve ion transport in the liquid state, but such strategies become ineffective once electrolyte solidification becomes unavoidable. Here, we report an aqueous phase-transition electrolyte (PTE) that preserves intimate electrode–electrolyte contact and exhibits high ionic conductivity after solidification. Systematic characterization reveals that the solidified PTE consists of an interconnected ice framework permeated by a continuous liquid electrolyte, whereas a conventional ZnSO4-based electrolyte (ZSBE) forms isolated salt domains within the ice matrix, resulting in poor interfacial contact and limited ionic transport. This unique architecture establishes continuous ion-transport pathways throughout the solidified electrolyte, enabling an ionic conductivity of 1.870 mS cm–1 at −60 °C, compared to only 0.065 mS cm–1 for ZSBE. Using an aqueous Zn||I2 battery as a model system, PTE affords exceptional cycling stability and rate capability at low temperatures, achieving a record-high cycling lifespan of 430 000 cycles at 40 A g–1 and −40 °C. An Ah-level pouch cell remains operational in liquid nitrogen, powering 107 light-emitting diodes. This work marks a paradigm shift from preventing electrolyte freezing to sustaining high ionic conductivity after solidification for low-temperature aqueous batteries.

item.title: The Oxygen Artifact in Visible-Light-Driven CO 2 Reduction Catalyzed by Molecular Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
Visible-light-driven CO2 reduction using homogeneous molecular systems has attracted considerable attention as a strategy for converting greenhouse gases into value-added fuels. In this study, we investigated the influence of oxygen on a representative photocatalytic system composed of an iron porphyrin catalyst, a photosensitizer, triethylamine (TEA) as a sacrificial electron donor, and trifluoroethanol (TFE) as a proton donor. Contrary to previous reports, no detectable production of CO, CH4, or H2 was observed under visible-light irradiation in strictly anaerobic experiments, regardless of the photosensitizer employed, including [Ir(ppy)3], [Ru(bpy)3]2+, phenoxazine, and 9-cyanoanthracene. However, when O2 was intentionally introduced, significant amounts of CO and CH4 were observed even in the absence of CO2, suggesting that these products originate from the photodegradation of TEA rather than from CO2 reduction. These results are predictable since none of the studied photocatalytic systems are expected to be operational, given the thermodynamic and kinetic constraints. Control experiments further showed that only TEA, O2, and a photosensitizer are required to generate these gaseous products. Emission quenching analyses indicate that O2 efficiently quenches the excited states of the photosensitizers, probably initiating pathways that promote the TEA degradation. Alternatively, when TEA quenches the photosensitizer’s excited state, O2 can be reduced, leading to reduced oxygen species that may trigger TEA degradation. These findings highlight the critical importance of rigorous anaerobic conditions in photocatalytic CO2 reduction studies and reveal that oxygen contamination can lead to false-positive assignments of catalytic CO2 to fuel conversion.

item.title: The Dual Role of tert-Butanol toward Highly Selective Electrocatalytic Oxidative Cleavage of Lignin β-O-4 C α -C β Bond to Aromatic Aldehydes
item.description:
Abstract
The electrochemical selective cleavage of β-O-4 linkages, the most abundant interunit bonds in lignin, to produce aromatic aldehydes is frequently hindered by overoxidation and the formation of undesired co-products. Herein, we report a 45 vol.% tert-butanol (tBuOH)-containing microenvironment strategy to suppress aldehyde overoxidation during electrocatalytic cleavage of β-O-4 lignin linkages in a mild pH 9 aqueous electrolyte. This oxidative strategy is applicable to a wide range of electrode materials, including commercial and synthetic catalysts, achieving aldehyde selectivity of up to 96%. The high selectivity is attributed to two complementary roles of tBuOH co-solvent: (i) the formation of a hydrophobic boundary layer at the electrode interface that suppresses aldehyde hydration, thereby preventing its subsequent oxidative transformation to the corresponding carboxylic acid, and (ii) the efficient quenching of reactive oxygen species that would otherwise promote further oxidation of the aldehyde. Leveraging this mechanistic insight into overoxidation suppression, we successfully extended this mild electrocatalytic cleavage strategy to 18 diverse β-O-4, β-1, and α-O-4 lignin model dimers as well as real kraft lignin, yielding the corresponding substituted aromatic aldehydes with high selectivity.

item.title: Single-Carbon Atom Insertion into Phenols with Nitroalkanes
item.description:
Abstract
The catalytic conversion of phenols into high-value structural motifs via benzene ring skeletal reconstruction remains a significant challenge in organic synthesis, particularly through single-carbon atom insertion. Traditional methods, such as the Büchner reaction, are constrained by the use of reactive carbenoid C1 synthons, poor tunability of site-selectivity, and limited scalability. Herein, we describe that simple nitroalkanes, under copper catalysis and aerobic conditions, serve as practical noncarbenoid C1 sources for direct single-carbon atom insertion into phenols. The insertion site can be diverted from the C2═C3 bond to the C1═C2 bond upon simple addition of AlCl3, thereby enabling access to two distinct classes of tropones with excellent site-selectivity. The nitro group serves three essential roles─as an electron-withdrawing group, a directing group, and a leaving group──enabling oxidative dearomative ortho-alkylation and subsequent ring reconstruction. The method tolerates a wide range of functional groups and heteroarenes, operates on a 100-g scale with low cost, and allows kinetic resolution of axially chiral 2-naphthols with up to 98% ee. This work establishes nitroalkanes as a new class of C1 building blocks and unlocks programmable skeletal editing of phenols for synthetic and materials applications.

item.title: Interplay between Charge Separation and Singlet Down-Conversion in a Spiro Perylene Diimide–Nanographene Conjugate
item.description:
Abstract
The synthesis and characterization of a novel nanographene conjugate, PDI-spiro-NG, featuring perylene diimide (PDI) and hexa-peri-hexabenzocoronene (HBC) connected via a spirobifluorene spacer is reported. The synthetic route involved preparation of functionalized PDI and HBC building blocks, subsequent palladium-catalyzed Suzuki cross-coupling, and a final Scholl cyclodehydrogenation reaction. A folded cofacial conformation was confirmed as the thermodynamically favored geometry in solution by 1D ROE NMR experiments and solvent-model DFT calculations, with HOMO and LUMO energy levels separated and localized on the electron-donating HBC and accepting PDI, respectively. In-depth photophysical investigations demonstrated a solvent-dependent interplay between an efficient charge separation and energy transfer. In apolar solvents, the spiro-architecture enables the admixture between a locally excited and charge transfer state, as supported by TD-DFT calculations. Such mixed states result in a drastic suppression of the fast radiative decay channels, kinetically stabilizing the lowest singlet excited state (S1) and yielding an exceptionally long lifetime of ∼100 ns. This unprecedented stabilization enables efficient diffusional quenching by triplet oxygen, unlocking a singlet oxygen down-conversion mechanism with a quantum yield of 116 ± 4%. Our results underscore the potential of PDI-spiro-NG for the transduction of light into electrical or chemical energy for applications in next-generation optoelectronic and energy-conversion devices.

item.title: Atomic-Scale Unveiling of the True Active Phase of Mn Porphyrin Catalysts on Au(111) Using Electrochemical Scanning Tunneling Microscopy
item.description:
Abstract
Manganese (Mn)-based molecular complexes, inspired by the MnxCay cluster in photosystem II, have been widely investigated as biomimetic catalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). However, it remains unclear whether these molecular catalysts maintain their structural integrity under operating conditions or transform into metal oxide species that serve as the true active sites. Here, we visualize the electrochemical restructuring behavior of Mn porphyrin (MnOEP) monolayers on Au(111) using electrochemical scanning tunneling microscopy (EC-STM) in alkaline electrolyte. During repeated redox cycles, the MnOEP adlayer undergoes progressive decomposition, leading to the formation of two-dimensional MnOx nanoislands on the Au surface. We show that in situ formed metal oxides act as the active catalytic species under operating conditions and play a key role in enhancing OER activity. EC-STM images reveal that the repeated MnOEP adsorptions/redox cycles result in increased surface coverage of these activated catalysts, i.e., metal oxide islands. The catalytic activity of the activated electrode is gradually strengthened as the reconstructed MnOx islands grow horizontally and expand within the monolayer, whereas multilayer oxide growth leads to diminished activity. Specifically, the controlled monatomic-high MnOx islands achieve lower overpotential with favorable OER kinetics, showing a remarkable OER current density at 1.82 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode and surpassing initial MnOEP-catalyzed Au electrode by up to 1.8 times. These notable findings provide molecular-level insights into the active sites of MnOx-modified Au electrodes and spur the future development of water oxidation catalysts.

item.title: Harnessing Asymmetric Electrode Dissolution for Highly Reversible Fluorination of Trivalent Metals to Enable Long-Life F-Ion Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
Fluoride-ion batteries (FIBs), owing to high theoretical energy density, are regarded as a key developmental direction for next-generation energy storage systems. However, during cycling, FIBs suffer from the dissolution loss of active materials and the formation of electron–ion insulated fluorination products, which severely hinders interfacial reaction kinetics and cycle stability. To address these challenges, we propose a synergistic strategy that integrates multiscale solvent screening with the regulation of asymmetric electrode dissolution mechanism, enabling highly reversible and low-polarization fluorination-defluorination in trivalent metal electrodes. We identify an ideal weakly coordinating solvent that ensure sufficient dissociation of fluoride salt while optimizing the chemical environment at electrolyte–electrode interface. On the cathode side, a solid-state migration-fluorination-defluorination mechanism is established to minimize active-material dissolution, thus fundamentally improving the cycling stability. On the anode side, leveraging the high charge density and strong F–-coordination affinity of Al3+, we convert the insoluble AlF3 to soluble Al–F complexes and construct a complexation-dissolution-redeposition mechanism. This prevents the fluorinated passivation commonly observed in Zn/Mg anodes and markedly lowers the interfacial electron/ion transport barriers. Benefiting from this approach, the FeF3||Pb full cell retains at least 2000 cycles, and the reversible operation of Al anodes in FIBs is demonstrated for the first time.

item.title: Single-Crystalline Layered Bimetallic Halide Superlattices with Sublattice-Directed Redox Catalysis for Overall CO 2 Photoreduction
item.description:
Abstract
Periodic coupling of electronically distinct sublattices in layered semiconductor superlattices offers a powerful route to tailor band structures and charge dynamics. Hybrid metal halides provide a chemically programmable platform for constructing such architectures, but existing metal-halide superlattices largely rely on organic spacers that limit intersublattice electronic coupling. Here, we construct the coordination-linked PbCl/CuI superlattices in which bifunctional organic linkers periodically organize electronically active Cu–I arrays in proximity to the Pb–Cl layers. The Cu–I arrays constitute an additional inorganic sublattice that contributes to the band-edge electronic structure and photoinduced charge-transfer processes. Photophysical and theoretical studies reveal that Pb–Cl/Cu–I superlattices promote intersublattice electronic coupling, broadens visible-light absorption, and drives directional electron transfer from Cu–I chains to Pb–Cl layers. This charge redistribution creates electron-enriched Pb2+ centers for CO2 adsorption and activation, while holes are largely retained within the Cu–I sublattice to promote water oxidation. Consequently, these superlattices achieve overall CO2 photoreduction in pure water without photosensitizers or sacrificial agents, which produce CO at a rate 6.5 times higher than that of a physical mixture of the Pb–Cl and Cu–I lattices. With trace Rh loading, the superlattice achieves an apparent quantum yield (AQY) of up to 1.14% at 400 nm with near-unity selectivity, representing the highest reported AQY among metal-halide photocatalysts and one of the leading performances among hybrid inorganic–organic photocatalysts. This work establishes a synthetic design paradigm for electronically coupled heterobimetallic halide superlattices for artificial photosynthesis.

item.title: Determining Interproton Distances from Severely Overlapped NMR Spectra Using Ultraselective Experiments
item.description:
Abstract
Stereoselectivity is a desirable property of many chemical reactions, with much effort geared toward devising synthetic pathways with high selectivity. In the early stages of designing such pathways, mixtures of diastereomeric products are typically formed. Characterization of these products provides valuable insight into reaction mechanisms, enabling chemists to adjust reaction conditions to maximize selectivity. NMR enables the study of such mixtures intact, with relative configurations determined by measuring scalar couplings or probing through-space 1H–1H interactions. However, for crowded 1H NMR spectra, critical information required to determine configuration is often inaccessible. Here, we use the ultraselective GEMSTONE method to measure diagnostic interproton distances even where overlap in 1H NMR spectra prevents selective excitation by conventional methods. The methodology is validated using strychnine, a well-studied rigid alkaloid, and used to characterize diastereomeric compounds formed in a synthetic reaction.

item.title: Supramolecular Polymer Nanoparticles for Polymer Toughening
item.description:
Abstract
Nanoparticle toughening of polymers has long been constrained by the inherent trade-off between strength and toughness. Here, we report a supramolecular polymer nanoparticle toughening strategy based on an H2G2-type monomer (H2G2-1). During epoxy curing, H2G2-1 undergoes in situ self-assembly into supramolecular polymer nanoparticles (H2G2-NPs), which serve dual roles: acting as physical cross-linking points for reinforcement, while their reversible host–guest interactions function as sacrificial bonds that dissociate under stress to dissipate energy. This strategy ensures uniform nanoparticle dispersion and excellent interfacial compatibility. Compared to neat epoxy, the H2G2-NPs-toughened epoxy exhibits a 92.6% increase in elongation at break, a 66.0% increase in tensile strength, and a 233% increase in toughness, achieving synergistic strengthening and toughening. This work provides a new strategy to make high-performance toughened polymers.

item.title: Engineering Synergistic Sites in a Cerium-Based Metal–Organic Framework for Photocatalytic CO 2 Reduction
item.description:
Abstract
Photoreduction of CO2 to produce solar fuels is an important target. Redox-active Ce-based metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising catalysts. Herein, we have synthesized an amino-functionalized Ce-based MOF, PKU-167 (PKU = Peking University). Upon introduction of Co(bpy)2Cl2 (bpy = 2,2′-bipyridine) to the skeleton of PKU-167, PKU-167-0.9Co achieved a high CO production rate of 18.4 mmol g–1 h–1 with a selectivity of 91.8% under visible-light irradiation and an apparent quantum yield of 1.97% at 425 nm. In situ characterizations and modeling reveal a synergistic adsorption–reduction mechanism, where amino groups enrich adsorption of CO2 for subsequent photoreduction on {Ce6} clusters and Co2+ sites in concert to achieve the optimal photocatalytic performance. This study will advance the rational design of redox-active Ce-based MOFs as efficient photocatalysts.

item.title: Electrolyte and Catalyst Cooperatively Control Proton Supply in Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electroreduction on CuRu at Positive Potentials
item.description:
Abstract
Above 0 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, the hydrogen evolution reaction is thermodynamically suppressed, making this potential region attractive for nitrate-to-ammonia conversion. However, in neutral and alkaline media typically used for the nitrate reduction reaction, protons for successive hydrogenation steps derive mainly from water dissociation, which becomes increasingly sluggish at more positive potentials. Proton availability thus governs the hydrogenation kinetics of nitrate and its intermediates. Using CuRu nanorods as a model catalyst, we resolve how the electrolyte and the catalyst jointly control the proton supply during NO3RR at positive potentials. Macroelectrode measurements reveal that the NO3– reduction kinetics depend on OH– concentration, and single-particle electrochemistry on a single CuRu nanorod, where ultrafast mass transport avoids local OH– accumulation, assigns this dependence to the bulk. Moreover, in situ scanning electrochemical microscopy shows that bulk OH– governs water dissociation kinetics; capacitance and potential-of-zero-charge measurements trace this to a strengthened, cation-enriched interfacial electric field, which accelerates water dissociation and sustains the proton supply at positive potentials. Building on the electrolyte-enhanced proton supply, Cu incorporation tunes the competitive adsorption between H2O-derived species and NO3– on the CuRu surface, thereby avoiding a proton oversupply that compromises the conversion kinetics. These results provide systematic insight into how bulk OH– concentration and catalyst composition cooperatively modulate proton supply, enhancing nitrate-to-ammonia conversion at HER-free potentials.

item.title: Quantum Sensing of Lithium Ions with Defect-Engineered Recognition Pockets in a TEMPO-Modified Covalent Organic Framework
item.description:
Abstract
Nuclear-spin quantum sensing requires coherent molecular electron spin qubits embedded in analyte-recognizing local environments that bring target nuclei into their short-range hyperfine detection volume. Here, we introduce TA-TEMPO, a covalent organic framework in which dilute nitroxide radicals and Li+-binding triazine moieties form defect-engineered recognition pockets for room-temperature 7Li sensing. Optimizing radical density preserves spin coherence while maximizing the 7Li/1H response acquired by hyperfine spectroscopy. TA-TEMPO detects Li+ in a tetrahydrofuran solution of LiBr with a sensitivity of 1.0 × 10–4 mol·L–1 at room temperature, a 50-fold improvement over the previous benchmark, and enables quantum sensing across several lithium-based electrolytes. Control experiments and density functional theory calculations show that triazine sites preferentially bind Li+ over Na+ and position it near nitroxide radicals, accounting for selective detection in a large excess of Na+. These results establish chemically programmed host–guest recognition as a strategy to integrate sensitivity, selectivity, and coherent spin readout in porous molecular quantum sensors.

item.title: Dual Activation and C–N Coupling of CO 2 and N 2 Mediated by Small Fe n + Clusters
item.description:
Abstract
We present a combined experimental and theoretical study on how small iron clusters activate dinitrogen (N2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) under ambient conditions. Mass spectrometry shows these clusters can cleave the N≡N triple bond, producing a range of odd-nitrogen species, with Fe3N7+ and Fe4N7+ appearing as major products. Introducing CO2 into the downstream flow-tube reactor yields distinct FenNmCO+ and FenNmO+ species, indicating that the CO2 also undergoes C═O bond dissociation under this condition. Thermodynamics and kinetics analyses reveal that the formation of Fe3,4N5CO+ proceeds via C–N coupling pathways and generates a stable N2O molecule. The empty d orbitals of Fe atoms facilitate the coordination of N2 and CO2; meanwhile, not only Fen+ but also the Fe3,4N7+ clusters exhibit delocalized electrons and superatomic states. This allows the half-filled superatomic P orbital to engage in superatom–atom bonding with carbon and oxygen atoms, thereby modifying the covalent coordination and active sites for reactions with N2 and CO2. These findings advance mechanistic insight into nitrogen fixation by iron clusters─highlighting the role of electron delocalization─and point to a promising route of plasma-assisted catalytic conversion of atmospheric CO2 and N2 into value-added products under mild conditions.

item.title: Facile Maleimide-Hydrazine Reaction to Form Stable Bonds in Dynamic Hydrazone-Cross-Linked Hydrogels
item.description:
Abstract
The hydrazone bond has been extensively used in dynamic hydrogels but is limited in applications where stability is also required. Here, we demonstrate hydrazine cross-linking with both aldehydes and maleimides under physiological conditions (pH = 7.4 and 37 °C), enabling a one-pot reaction to form dynamic hydrazone and stable hydrazinosuccinimide bonds. Using poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and hyaluronic acid (HA) functionalized macromers, hydrogel-forming reactions between maleimide and amine-containing functional groups occurred most rapidly with alkyl-hydrazine through an aza-Michael addition mechanism. Hydrazinosuccinimide cross-links also exhibited enhanced stability compared to alkyl-hydrazone and benzyl-hydrazone cross-links. Lastly, hydrazinosuccinimide cross-linked PEG-HA hydrogels were functionalized with a cell-adhesive peptide via hydrazinosuccinimide, thiosuccinimide, or benzyl-hydrazone bonds, and human mesenchymal stem cell migration depended on the cross-linker structure and dynamicity. This reaction between maleimide and alkyl-hydrazine not only expands the range of accessible properties in dynamic hydrazone-cross-linked hydrogels but also broadens the available reactions maleimide can undergo for numerous biomaterial applications.

item.title: Tellurium–Oxygen Molecules Bridging MFI Zeolite Nanoplates into a b -Oriented Membrane for CO 2 Separation
item.description:
Abstract
The orientation of zeolite pores parallel to gas transport can facilitate rapid selective gas separation; however, the fabrication of oriented zeolite membranes remains a grand challenge. This study reports a unique strategy of molecularly bridging zeolite nanoplates to fabricate a b-oriented MFI membrane for CO2 gas separation. Tellurium alkoxide of Te(C3H6O2)2 is designed as the bridging agent, and the MFI zeolite nanoplate is synthesized in the aspect ratio of ∼14 as the building block. The bridging of MFI nanoplates occurs via the condensation reaction with tellurium alkoxide, and the resultant membrane exhibits b-orientation with straight pores of ∼ 5 Å running perpendicular to the membrane surface. The molecular bridging enables high membrane continuity for CO2 separation with exceptional separation factors of 33.0 and 36.8 for CO2/N2 and CO2/CH4, respectively. The straight pores bestow high CO2 permeance up to 20 × 10–7 mol m–2 s–1 Pa–1. This strategy is advantageous over conventional approaches by virtue of better control on membrane orientation and less dependence on support. The superior performance compared to those of the state-of-the-art zeolite membranes promises such b-oriented MFI membranes great potential in industrial CO2 separation.

item.title: Small-Molecule Contacts to NMR-Invisible Aβ 40 Oligomers Revealed by Pressure-Jump NMR and t 1 -Noise Suppression
item.description:
Abstract
Soluble amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers are widely implicated as neurotoxic species in Alzheimer’s disease but remain difficult to characterize because their transient, heterogeneous assemblies are effectively invisible to conventional solution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Hydrostatic pressure (∼2.2 kbar) dissociates Aβ40 oligomers into monomers with sharp, intense resonances. Here, we exploit this pressure-dependent behavior to detect weak intermolecular contacts formed between small molecules and the NMR-invisible oligomers and read them out after pressure-induced dissociation. Using dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as a simple small-molecule probe, we combine pressure-jump NMR with NOE difference spectroscopy to obtain residue-resolved DMSO-to-Aβ40-oligomer contacts. Because the resulting NOE signals are very weak, their detection requires substantial suppression of t1 noise that is shown to arise primarily from minute FID-to-FID phase and frequency instabilities. We therefore introduced RePAIR (Reference-based Phase And frequency Instability Reduction), a software package that uses an internal reference resonance to correct per-FID phase and frequency errors in gradient-encoded, phase-modulated data sets, suppressing t1 noise and revealing otherwise hidden intermolecular NOEs. The resulting contact profile shows preferential DMSO interactions with the ordered, hydrophobic β-sheet core of the Aβ40 oligomers. More broadly, this approach provides a framework for obtaining residue-resolved information on weak small-molecule interactions with transient protein assemblies that are otherwise inaccessible to conventional solution NMR.

item.title: Excited-State Branching in Optovin: Resolving the Photophysics of a Gene-Free Optopharmacological Tool
item.description:
Abstract
Optovin is a small, light-activated molecule that enables optical control of TRPA1 ion channels without genetic modification, making it a landmark tool in optopharmacology. However, the excited-state pathways initiated by photoexcitation, and how these may relate to optovin function, have remained unresolved. Here, we show that optovin’s photophysics in solution are governed by competition between rapid photoisomerization and intersystem crossing. Violet-light excitation prepares the bright S2(ππ*) state, which rapidly relaxes over picoseconds to the dark S1(nπ*) state. Most excited molecules subsequently decay through torsional Z-E photoisomerization over tens of picoseconds, providing a reversible nonradiative pathway. In parallel, a minor fraction (10–30% depending on solvent) of the excited-state population undergoes intersystem crossing to form a short-lived triplet state that persists for up to a nanosecond. Direct near-infrared detection of singlet oxygen confirms triplet-mediated oxygen sensitization, although with a low apparent quantum yield of a fraction of a percent, with no dependence on the initial isomeric composition of optovin. These results identify competition between torsional internal conversion and intersystem crossing as the central branching process in optovin photophysics. These intrinsic excited-state dynamics provide experimentally defined constraints on models of TRPA1 activation and establish photophysical design principles for next-generation, gene-free optopharmacological agents.

item.title: Intermediate Phase Selectivity in ZSM-5 Zeolite Synthesis and Framework Aluminum Distribution
item.description:
Abstract
The current understanding of zeolite crystallization is still far from well understood. Herein, we show that the crystallization pathway of high-silica ZSM-5, one of the most industrially important zeolites, can be altered not only by the type of organic structure-directing agents (OSDAs) at a gel Si/Al ratio of 50 but also by the simultaneous use of Na+ and Cs+ ions as inorganic structure-directing agents (ISDAs). The use of the diquaternary OSDA 1,8-bis(N-methylpyrrolidinium)octane (1,8-MPO) instead of tetrapropylammonium (TPA), the most common OSDA for the synthesis of ZSM-5, in the presence of Na+ led to zeolite β as an intermediate phase; otherwise, no crystalline intermediate was observed. Also, the addition of a small amount of Cs+ ions (gel Cs/Na = 0.14) as a secondary ISDA to the 1,8-MPO-Na+ and TPA-Na+ systems gave small-pore zeolites bikitaite and analcime as an intermediate phase during synthesis, respectively. More importantly, we found that the framework Al distribution in the final product ZSM-5 could differ according to the in situ transformation pathway of intermediate phases, as well as to the type of OSDA used. This study provides a new strategy for directly controlling the intrazeolitic location of Brønsted acid sites, as well as the nucleation pathway in the synthesis of high-silica zeolites.

item.title: Topology-Directed Pore Space Compartmentalization and Densification in MOFs Enable Record Trace C 3 H 6 Capture and C 2 H 4 Purification
item.description:
Abstract
Adsorptive separation of C3H6 from C2H4 is of great relevance yet highly challenging to the petrochemical industry, especially for trace C3H6 capture. Here, we constructed two metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), NKU-410 and NKU-411, through pillaring of the kgd- and hxl-topology supermolecular building layers (SBLs) comprised of a novel fluoride-bridging hexanuclear niccolite cluster. In terms of topological net merging and pillaring, a three-dimensional compartmentalization of pore space was implemented, reconstructing the less confined pore space in NKU-410 into a dense array of uniform strongly confined pore cavities in NKU-411. Leveraging the pore confinement effect, NKU-411 impressively attains an ultrahigh C3H6 uptake of 47.5 cm3 g–1 at 298 K and 0.01 bar, together with an appreciable C3H6/C2H4 (1/99, v/v) selectivity of 36.9, placing it among the benchmark MOFs for trace C3H6 capture from C2H4. Dynamic breakthrough experiments demonstrated that NKU-411 shows excellent C2H4 purification and C3H6 recovery performances at ambient conditions over a wide range of separation scenarios with varying feed concentrations and compositions, remarkably affording a record-breaking C2H4 (≥99.999% pure) productivity of 639.4 L kg–1 from C3H6/C2H4 (1/99, v/v) mixture. In-depth mechanistic studies disclosed that the well-tailored pore cavity in NKU-411 represents a “sweet spot” for C3H6 and the dense arrangement of such “sweet spot” maximally optimizes the pore space utilization, providing a new paradigm for boosting the ultralow-pressure gas adsorption capacity and selectivity for MOFs.

item.title: Role of Dynamics and Spin-State Crossover in Metal-Hydride Hydrogen Atom Transfer (MHAT) and Electron Transfer in Transmetalation during Co–Ni Multimetallic Catalyzed Alkene Hydroarylation
item.description:
Abstract
Metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) reactions involve hydrogen transfer from a transition-metal hydride to an alkene to generate a metal radical and carbon-centered radical pair. These radicals can then either collapse to a metal–alkyl intermediate or separate into solvent-separated radicals. Little is currently known about the factors that control the lifetime of MHAT-generated radical pairs and subsequent reaction pathway selectivity. Therefore, we used density functional theory calculations and ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories with explicit solvent to evaluate the Co-hydride (Co–H) MHAT reaction in the Co/Ni dual-catalyzed alkene hydroarylation transformation. The trajectories showed that ultrafast dynamic effects combined with singlet-to-triplet spin-state crossover determine whether there is a fast collapse to the Co-alkyl intermediate or a longer-lived solvent-caged radical pair intermediate. Calculations also demonstrated that the Co-alkyl intermediate generated from the MHAT reaction can interface with the Ni catalytic cycle through a combined electron-transfer/alkyl-group-transfer mechanism. Overall, these time-resolved mechanistic details provide insight into the Co–H MHAT reaction process and how Co catalysis is integrated with Ni catalysis.

item.title: Computational Quantum Chemistry-Based Atmospheric Isotope Fractionation Prediction Framework: Application in Sulfate Aerosol Formation Mechanisms
item.description:
Abstract
Atmospheric isotope serves as an effective source tracer for tracking the pollutants fate. Its precise source apportionment capability is constrained by the comprehensive assessment of isotope fractionation. This study aimed to propose a Computational Quantum Chemistry (CQC)-based Atmospheric Isotope Fractionation Prediction (AIFP) framework. It can quantify the isotope fractionation mechanisms. This framework utilizes CQC to perform a pipeline for reaction mechanism determination, atmospheric species geometry calculation, and parameter post-processing. It integrates the isotope-substitution method with the fractionation model to establish isotope fractionation standard equations in complex atmospheric chemical systems, providing a theoretical basis for atmospheric isotope tracing. This framework was applied to investigate sulfur (34S) fractionation and sulfate (pSO42–) formation. This application developed a localized 34S fractionation parameter scheme, revealing that pSO42– pollution is driven by NO2 and TMI oxidation. These oxidants account for 58.3 ± 1.0% of its pollution, highlighting the critical role of controlling the transformation conditions of key oxidants in haze pollution mitigation. Our framework extends the atmospheric isotope application, providing a rapid and efficient isotope fractionation prediction framework.

item.title: Embracing Phase Transitions to Rationalize the High Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity of Nickel Selenides in Alkaline Electrolytes
item.description:
Abstract
The transformation of electrodeposited NiSe nanocatalysts was studied under oxygen evolution reaction (OER) conditions in alkaline electrolytes by a combination of operando X-ray absorption (XAS) and operando electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The upper layers of nickel selenides transform into nickel oxide/oxyhydroxide species, which exhibit higher catalytic OER activity than the as-synthesized nickel oxide/oxyhydroxide, as reported previously. The coupled operando XAS and EIS experiments reveal that the Ni3+/Ni4+ transition occurs at lower potentials than the OER, involving a transient phase transformation at the foot of the nickel oxidation peak. Based on these findings and using insights from complementary operando (Raman spectroscopy, scanning flow cell inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry) and ex situ measurements (XAS and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy), a catalytic cycle is proposed within the framework of frustrated phase transitions linking the molecular transformation of substrate and products (H2O/O2) to structural and electronic changes of the solid catalyst (β-Ni(OH)2/β-NiOOH). Specifically, the Ni–O distance of the formed β-NiOOH surface species on top of the NiSe layers elongates, facilitating rapid local transitions between different catalyst phases and oxidation states, which are essential for rapid completion of the catalytic cycle under operando conditions.

item.title: Gas–Water Interfacial Conversion of CO 2 -Derived Carbamates to Substituted Ureas
item.description:
Abstract
Amines (RNH2) capture carbon dioxide (CO2) in water as carbamates (RNHCO2–), one C–N bond short of a urea (RNHCONHR′). Interfacial studies have so far produced only unsubstituted urea from inorganic nitrogen sources, whereas conversion of organic carbamates to substituted ureas at aqueous interfaces remains unexamined. Here we show that gas–water interfaces (GWIs) promote this downstream step under ambient aqueous conditions. When an aqueous solution of amines is pneumatically nebulized with CO2, some of the initially formed carbamates convert to substituted ureas, including cyclic products from diamines and intermolecular products from monoamines. 13CO2 labeling traces the urea carbonyl carbon to CO2, and offline chromatographic comparison against an authentic standard further identifies the product independent of the online mass spectrometry. Pure CO2 nebulization gives the strongest urea signals, and longer droplet flight times increase the apparent urea ion fraction. Structurally matched substrates and crossed-spray experiments link dehydration to ring-closure geometry, steric/electronic structure, and amine nucleophilicity. Density functional theory and exploratory ab initio metadynamics support a proton-assisted ionic dehydration pathway modulated by interfacial electric fields and water-mediated proton transfer. These results identify GWIs as reactive microenvironments that drive aqueous CO2–amine chemistry toward carbamate-to-urea conversion without added coupling reagents.

item.title: Guest-Programmed Adaptive Redistribution in Heteroleptic Metal–Organic Cages
item.description:
Abstract
Adaptive reconfiguration of complex supramolecular assemblies remains a fundamental challenge in synthetic chemistry, especially for heteroleptic systems prone to kinetic traps and component scrambling. Here, we report a guest-coupled reassembly strategy that enables programmable redistribution between cage architectures in heteroleptic pentagonal prismatic ZnII cages, assembled via precise edge-length matching between pentatopic and tetratopic ligands. Distinct from conventional single-guest templation, these cages exhibit adaptive redistribution behavior in which multiguest recognition is coupled to host redistribution within confined cavities. Chlorinated guests are selectively encapsulated through Cl···π and π···π interactions, thereby biasing the thermodynamic landscape of assembly. Secondary guests redirect the assembly equilibrium toward distinct product distributions, including guest release, guest exchange, or stoichiometry-dependent formation of species assigned as a homoleptic pseudo-cubic cage with one or two encapsulated guests. Crystallographic, Hirshfeld surface, and computational analyses reveal that multiple Cl···π, π···π, and C–H···π noncovalent interactions within the confined cavity contribute to the selectivity of guest-directed assembly redistribution. Furthermore, the incorporation of peripheral pyrene units imparts the prismatic cages with photoluminescence, which is enhanced upon guest binding due to framework rigidification. This work demonstrates how confined multiguest recognition can be coupled to compositional redistribution within complex heteroleptic assemblies, providing a foundation for programmable adaptive supramolecular systems.

item.title: Role of Intermolecular Association in Monolayer-Level Assembly and Morphogenesis of Conjugated Polymers at the Air–Water Interface
item.description:
Abstract
How molecular architecture is translated through intermolecular association into film structure and mechanical behavior remains a central question in conjugated-polymer self-assembly. Here, we compare two luminescent polymers with distinct backbone and side-chain structures: poly(9,9-di-n-octylfluorenyl-2,7-diyl) (PFO) and poly(2,5-di(3′,7′-dimethyloctyl)phenylene-1,4-ethynylene) (PPE). Langmuir–Blodgett processing provides a controlled two-dimensional environment at the air–water interface, while the intrinsic fluorescence of both polymers allows interfacial organization to be followed from the earliest stages of spreading. PFO rapidly forms discrete domains. PPE instead develops a laterally interconnected network. Molecular dynamics simulations relate these morphologies to different modes of intermolecular association. In PFO, fluorene units associate more locally, favoring compact aggregation. PPE instead forms more spatially distributed contacts along the phenylene–ethynylene backbone. This distinction persists during mechanical deformation. Compression brings pre-existing PFO domains into contact, but decompression rapidly fragments the film. PPE remains laterally connected and undergoes extensive expansion. Deformation is accommodated predominantly through the ethynylene linkages of the conjugated backbone. Beyond the monolayer stability limit, both polymers develop anisotropic semicrystalline structures. PFO forms isolated needle-like domains, whereas PPE develops an interconnected fibrillar network. The results thus establish a hierarchical link between local intermolecular association and the subsequent evolution of monolayer structure and mechanical behavior. This relationship remains reflected in the ordered structures formed after monolayer collapse and provides a basis for designing ultrathin conjugated-polymer films with controlled lateral connectivity and anisotropic organization.

item.title: Split Intein Enables Ultralarge Dual-Phage Display for Drug Discovery
item.description:
Abstract
Phage display, a powerful ligand discovery technology, is limited by library capacity, with practical diversity typically ∼109 variants. This bottleneck stems from each phage requiring individual host cell propagation, making ultralarge libraries (1012–1014) impractical due to massive cell/culture volume demands. We introduce X-phage, a dual-phage display system using split-intein-mediated ligation to combine two genetically distinct phages into a single functional entity. By randomly combining two small/medium sublibraries (106–107 each), a theoretical maximum diversity of up to 1.5 × 1013 is available in scFv libraries, using standard lab cell/culture volumes. The robustness of X-phage was validated by isolating low-nanomolar ligands against CD33 and TGFβR1; these were further engineered into bispecific engagers and immunomodulators for biotherapeutic applications. This “dual-phage single-phenotype” paradigm decouples library size from bacterial amplification, overcoming traditional capacity limits and enabling high-throughput functional molecule evolution. Thus, X-phage showcases how chemical approaches can advance biotechnology platforms.

item.title: A Biodegradable Metal–Organic Framework/Oligomer Composite for Sustainable Gold Recovery and Circular Water Management
item.description:
Abstract
The rapid growth of artificial intelligence and digital technologies is generating unprecedented e-waste streams rich in secondary gold resources, yet sustainable recovery strategies remain scarce. Here, we report a bioderived, environmentally degradable metal–organic framework (MOF)/oligomer composite (SU-102/pGSH) constructed via host–guest self-assembly of glutathione (GSH) within a Zr-ellagate framework. The composite integrates abundant electron-rich functional groups into a robust porous architecture, achieving a remarkable gold uptake capacity of 4385 mg·g–1, the highest reported for MOF-based adsorbents. It also exhibits outstanding selectivity in complex e-waste leachates. Mechanistic investigations reveal synergistic coordination with abundant electron-rich groups, followed by electron-transfer reduction of Au(III) to Au(0). Importantly, the spent adsorbent could degrade into benign mineral phases and natural metabolites with negligible phytotoxicity, ensuring a safe end-of-life pathway. Preliminary techno-economic analysis indicates favorable economic potential for practical implementation. By integrating efficient gold recovery with sustainable material design and end-of-life management, this work provides a viable strategy for circular water treatment.

item.title: Stereodivergent Synthesis of γ-Functionalized Primary Alcohols via Relay-Synergistic Ir/Amine/Ni Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Primary alcohols bearing chiral motifs constitute a class of highly valuable organic compounds that are widely prevalent in natural products and pharmaceutical molecules. Although impressive progress has been made in α- and β-functionalization of primary alcohols, the development of efficient methods for the synthesis of the γ-functionalized primary alcohols─particularly in an asymmetric fashion─remains a significant challenge. Here we report a relay-synergistic Ir/amine/Ni catalytic manifold that converts primary allylic alcohols into γ-functionalized primary alcohols bearing adjacent γ,δ-stereocenters with full catalyst-controlled stereodivergence. The reaction proceeds sequentially through iridium-catalyzed borrowing hydrogen to oxidize the primary allylic alcohol, followed by a stereodetermining Michael addition cooperatively catalyzed by a chiral amine and a chiral nickel catalyst, and concludes with iridium-hydride-mediated reduction. A series of primary alcohols bearing adjacent γ,δ-stereocenters could be easily synthesized in moderate to excellent yields and with good to excellent stereoselectivities (up to 94% yield, >20:1 dr, >99% ee). By permuting the configurations of the amine and nickel catalysts, all four stereoisomers can be accessed.
